newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels free two more hostages, 81 left.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels free two more hostages, 81 left.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas holding VIP hostages at the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima freed two diplomats on Tuesday.
The released hostages were Honduran ambassador Jose Eduardo Martell Mejia and Argentine consul general Juan Ibanez, according to Red Cross official Michel Minnig, chief mediator in the crisis.
Apparently in good health, they walked out dressed in suits and carrying plastic bags with personal belongings. The immaculate-looking Ibanez, still wearing a tie, waved at waiting reporters.
The two men hugged Red Cross officials before getting into a police car that sped away.
The release of the envoys left the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) holding diplomats from only two foreign countries -- Japan and Bolivia -- among their remaining 81 captives.

The rebels have released more than 420 hostages since the crisis began Dec. 17, but they have kept those men they consider the best bargaining chips in negotiations over the release of their imprisoned comrades.

The government of neighbouring Bolivia holds several MRTA members in their jails but has refused to give in to the guerrillas' demands for releases in exchange for the freeing of ambassador Jorge Gumucio.
The 20-odd Japanese still captive include the ambassador Morihisa Aoki, four lower ranking embassy officials and businessmen.
All the remaining hostages were Peruvian, including two ministers, top security force officials, diplomats, congressmen and President Alberto Fujimor's brother, Pedro.

The latest release was immediately followed by the entrance into the residence of Catholic bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, who has acted as an observer in negotiations between the rebels and the government.

His stately entrance and the dignified exit of the two freed diplomats contrasted with the bustle of activity that dominated the siege site earlier on Tuesday, when the rebels staged impromptu interviews for two hours at the residence with a score of journalists.
Welcoming the media into the mined and booby-trapped compound for the first time since the beginnning of the siege, they also allowed the reporters to interview hostages.
